chapters.title: Our Green Little Garden
chapters.description: Delightful early reading and discovery in Nature Studies

pages.title: Welcome to the Green Garden
bulletPoints: The garden is a living paradise where soil, rain, warm sun, and fresh air work together.
Every towering oak and sweet juicy tomato began as a tiny, humble seed.
Gardening teaches patience, gentle care, and gratitude for the earth.
Put on your garden gloves, grab your watering can, and let's explore!
pages.footerText: Page 1 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Tiny Magic Seeds: Life in a Shell
bulletPoints: A seed looks like a dry, sleeping pebble, but inside lies an embryo plant waiting for water.
Seed coat: A tough protective armor keeping the baby plant safe from frost and heat.
Food store (Endosperm): Packed with starch and nutrients to feed the baby plant until leaves grow.
Variety: Tiny poppy seeds, smooth melon seeds, and large furrowed peach stones.
pages.footerText: Page 2 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Preparing the Soil: The Earth’s Bed
bulletPoints: Healthy soil is alive! It contains minerals, decaying organic compost, air, and moisture.
Loosening the ground: Use a small trowel to break up hard clods so tender roots can spread.
Compost magic: Dark rich compost made from dry leaves and vegetable peels feeds soil microbes.
Earthworms at work: Friendly worms burrow channels through soil, bringing oxygen to deep roots.
pages.footerText: Page 3 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Planting the Seed: Tucking It to Sleep
bulletPoints: The Golden Rule of Planting: Plant seeds at a depth equal to two or three times their thickness.
Tiny carrot seeds need only a light dusting of soil; large bean seeds sleep two inches deep.
Spacing rows: Leave enough room between seeds so growing plants will not crowd each other.
Gentle pat: Pat the soil down lightly so moisture can touch the seed coat on all sides.
pages.footerText: Page 4 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: A Gentle Drink: Watering the Garden
bulletPoints: Seeds need moisture to soften their hard coats and signal that spring has arrived.
Gentle rose nozzle: Use a showerhead nozzle so heavy water drops don't wash tiny seeds away.
Watering at sunrise: Morning is best because the soil stays moist before the hot midday sun.
Deep watering: It is better to water deeply twice a week than shallowly every day.
pages.footerText: Page 5 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Germination: The Awakening Root
bulletPoints: As the seed drinks water, it swells and the hard coat cracks open.
The Radicle: The very first part to emerge is a tender white root pointing straight down.
Geotropism: Gravity guides roots downward into the earth to find water and anchor the plant.
Microscopic root hairs: Thousands of tiny hairs absorb water and dissolved soil minerals.
pages.footerText: Page 6 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: The First Green Sprout: Pushing to the Light
bulletPoints: Phototropism: Stems naturally bend and grow upward toward bright sunlight.
Arching loop: The young stem forms a protective hook to push through heavy soil without damaging leaves.
Breaking through: A delicate green loop pokes through the brown dirt into the warm sunshine!
First sight: The pale sprout turns vivid emerald green within hours as chlorophyll forms.
pages.footerText: Page 7 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Cotyledons: The Seed Leaves
bulletPoints: The very first leaves that open are called cotyledons (seed leaves).
They look smooth and rounded, unlike the mature leaves that will follow later.
Food providers: They feed the baby plant using stored seed food until true leaves grow.
Once true leaves appear, cotyledons wither and fall off naturally, having completed their duty.
pages.footerText: Page 8 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: True Leaves & Photosynthesis
bulletPoints: True leaves emerge above the cotyledons with the characteristic shape of the adult plant.
Photosynthesis: Leaves are solar-powered sugar factories inside plant cells.
Ingredients: Green chlorophyll traps sunlight; roots provide water; leaves breathe carbon dioxide.
The gift: Plants create glucose food for themselves and release pure oxygen for us to breathe!
pages.footerText: Page 9 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Stems: The Highway of Sap
bulletPoints: The stem holds leaves high to catch maximum sunlight and supports heavy flowers and fruit.
Xylem tubes: One-way microscopic pipes carrying water and minerals up from the roots.
Phloem tubes: Two-way pipes carrying sugary sap from leaves to growing roots and shoots.
Herbaceous vs woody stems: Soft green daisy stems vs sturdy brown oak tree trunks.
pages.footerText: Page 10 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Deep Roots: Anchors in the Storm
bulletPoints: Taproots: A thick, deep main root reaching far underground (like carrots and dandelions).
Fibrous roots: A web of thin, branching roots spreading wide like a net (like grass and wheat).
Soil protectors: Dense roots hold soil tight, preventing heavy rains from washing soil into rivers.
Underground storage: Carrots, beets, and radishes store sugary food in roots for next year.
pages.footerText: Page 11 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Flower Buds: Nature's Wrapped Gifts
bulletPoints: When the plant reaches adulthood, it prepares to reproduce by forming tight flower buds.
Sepals: Small green leaflike shields that wrap the bud tight and protect delicate petals.
Swelling colors: As petals develop inside, glimpses of red, yellow, pink, and purple peek through.
Sunbeam trigger: Warm morning warmth encourages the sepals to peel back and bloom open!
pages.footerText: Page 12 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Blossoms Open: Color, Perfume & Nectar
bulletPoints: Petals: Colorful billboards designed to catch the attention of passing flying insects.
Sweet nectar: A sugary, fragrant syrup hidden deep inside the flower base as an insect treat.
Stamens & Pistils: The male stamens produce powdery yellow pollen; the female pistil receives it.
Fragrance in the breeze: Rose, jasmine, and honeysuckle perfume fills the summer garden air.
pages.footerText: Page 13 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: The Pollinators: Bees, Butterflies & Birds
bulletPoints: Honeybees fly from blossom to blossom, gathering nectar to make sweet golden honey in hives.
Pollen baskets: Bees brush against stamens; yellow pollen dusts their hairy legs and bodies.
Pollination: When the bee visits the next flower, pollen rubs off onto the sticky pistil.
Without bees and butterflies pollinating flowers, apples, berries, and pumpkins could never grow!
pages.footerText: Page 14 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: From Flower to Fruit: The Growing Pod
bulletPoints: Once a flower is pollinated, the colorful petals have completed their job and fall to the ground.
The ovary swells: The base of the flower begins to expand into a green fruit or seed pod.
Protective cradle: The fruit grows around the new developing seeds to shelter them from frost.
Ripening colors: As sunshine warms the fruit, it turns from sour hard green to sweet juicy red or yellow.
pages.footerText: Page 15 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Underground Treasures: Root Vegetables
bulletPoints: Pulling carrots: Grab the feathery green tops near the soil and pull straight up with a gentle tug.
Surprise: A crisp, bright orange carrot emerges fresh from the dark soil!
Radishes: Round ruby globes that grow in just 25 days from seed to harvest.
Potatoes: Digging with a garden fork unearths a treasure chest of golden potatoes under one vine.
pages.footerText: Page 16 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Climbing Vines: Tendrils Reaching High
bulletPoints: Peas and runner beans are climbing vines that love to reach high toward the blue sky.
Tendrils: Specialized curling threads that lash around bamboo canes and garden trellises.
Touch sensitive: When a tendril touches a pole, it rapidly curls into a tight spring coil to pull the stem up.
Sweet peas: Dainty fragrant purple blossoms cascading down the garden fence.
pages.footerText: Page 17 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Aromatic Herbs: Kitchen Scents
bulletPoints: Brush your hands through the herb bed to release essential oils into the air.
Mint: Cool, refreshing leaves that make invigorating summer iced teas.
Basil: Sweet, spicy green leaves that pair wonderfully with ripe garden tomatoes.
Rosemary: Needle-like evergreen leaves that smell like a pine forest and flavor roasted potatoes.
Lavender: Soft purple spikes with a calming scent that helps everyone relax and sleep.
pages.footerText: Page 18 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: Autumn Seed Saving: The Circle of Life
bulletPoints: In autumn, sunflower heads droop heavy with hundreds of striped black-and-white seeds.
Drying seeds: Cut mature sunflower heads and hang them in a dry shed to cure.
Harvesting: Rub seed heads over a bowl; seeds tumble out by the hundreds!
Saving for spring: Store dry seeds in labeled paper envelopes to plant next year's garden.
pages.footerText: Page 19 of 20 · Our Green Little Garden

pages.title: The Garden Feast: Gratitude for Nature
bulletPoints: Gathering the harvest: A wicker basket filled with tomatoes, cucumbers, carrots, and sweet peas.
Garden salads: Nothing tastes as delicious as vegetables harvested five minutes before dinner.
Lessons of the soil: Kindness, regular care, patience, and love bring abundant beauty to life.
Thank you, Earth: May our green garden bloom with joy, color, and life for seasons to come!
